question: In infection control, what do we call a non-living object like a stethoscope or door handle that can pass germs from one person to another?

options.C: The natural home of a pathogen
options.D: A break in the human skin

explanation: Spot on! In nursing, we call these non-living items 'fomites'. They easily pick up germs in the ward and carry them to the next patient if we don't clean our hands or equipment. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h1)

question: Why is the chain of infection like a link fence? What happens if you break just one link?

options.A: Pathogens require all six links to survive inside a reservoir
options.B: Breaking any single link stops the infection from spreading
options.C: The immune system only attacks pathogens when all links are full
options.D: Microorganisms multiply faster when every link is connected

explanation: You've got it! Think of infection control as stopping a chain reaction. If you wash your hands or clean a surface, you break the chain of transmission and stop the disease in its tracks. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h1)

question: A patient comes in with ringworm on their arm. What type of germ causes this common skin condition?
explanation: Correct! Don't let the name fool you—ringworm is caused by a fungus, not an actual worm. It loves warm, damp skin spots! [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h2)

question: During which stage of an infection does a patient feel just a bit 'off' with vague, mild symptoms, yet they easily spread the illness to others because they're still walking around?
explanation: Spot on! The prodromal stage is tricky because the patient just feels mildly tired or scratchy-throated, so they keep moving about and unknowingly share germs with everyone. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h3)

question: What is actually happening inside the body during the incubation period of an infectious disease?

options.A: Early, non-specific fatigue and body aches first start to show
options.B: The patient experiences the peak physical signs of the illness
options.C: Acute symptoms fade and body tissues begin to repair themselves
options.D: The pathogen multiplies inside the body without causing symptoms

explanation: You nailed it! During the incubation period, the germs have entered and are quietly throwing a party inside, multiplying until there are enough to finally make the patient feel sick. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h3)

question: Why does a cut or infected area of skin suddenly become red, warm, and swollen?

options.A: Pathogens are multiplying rapidly and blocking normal blood flow
options.B: Lymphocytes are actively producing antibodies inside the tissue
options.C: Stomach acid and tears are leaking into the subcutaneous tissue
options.D: Blood vessels dilate to bring white blood cells to the site

explanation: Spot on! That redness and warmth are signs of your body sending extra blood carrying rescue white blood cells straight to the battleground to fight the infection. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h4)

question: When checking lab results, which finding usually tells you the patient's body is actively fighting off an infection?
explanation: You got it! A high white blood cell count (leukocytosis) means the bone marrow is pumping out extra soldiers to tackle invading germs. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h5)

question: A patient has a painful surgical wound oozing foul-smelling yellow fluid. What test should the nurse expect the doctor to order first?
explanation: Correct! A wound culture lets the lab identify the exact troublemaker germ and figure out which antibiotic will wipe it out best. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h5)

question: What is the single most important and effective habit for stopping infections from spreading in any hospital or clinic?
explanation: Spot on! Simple, regular handwashing or hand sanitizing is your #1 defense against carrying germs from one patient to another. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h6)

question: A patient is admitted to the ward with active pulmonary tuberculosis (TB). What kind of isolation precautions must you set up right away?
explanation: You nailed it! Because TB germs float around in tiny particles in the air, you need a negative-pressure room and an N95 respirator mask to stay safe. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h6)

question: What actually is sepsis?

options.A: The initial stage of viral reproduction in a host cell
options.B: A localized skin reaction caused by fungal overgrowth
options.C: A systemic, life-threatening response to an infection
options.D: A normal immune reaction during the prodromal phase

explanation: Correct! Sepsis happens when an infection gets out of hand, triggering a severe, dangerous full-body inflammatory response that needs emergency care. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h7)

question: Which clinical sign tells you a patient is slipping into dangerous septic shock?

options.A: Localized redness and swelling around a surgical incision
options.B: High white blood cell count without any fever present
options.C: Dangerously low blood pressure unresponsive to fluids
options.D: Increased urine output caused by excessive fluid intake

explanation: Spot on! In septic shock, blood vessels relax so much that blood pressure plummets dangerously low and stubbornly refuses to bounce back, even after giving IV fluids. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h7)
